name: Sunrise alarm clock
lead: A sunrise alarm clock, also called a wake-up light or dawn simulator, is a bedside lamp that brightens gradually over roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours before a set wake time to imitate dawn, and often adds an optional sound alarm and a dimming dusk mode for bedtime [1]. Because light passes through closed eyelids, the sleeper is exposed to rising illumination before waking [1].

Dawn simulation has a clinical history in the treatment of winter seasonal depression, with trials from the 1980s onward [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and sleep-optimisation communities the devices are promoted for easier waking and a regular schedule, on the reasoning that consistent sleep supports appearance.

Published trials mostly involve patients with seasonal or winter depression and use specific protocols; results are mixed and samples are small. Evidence for healthy sleepers using commercial wake-up lights at home is limited in the sources reviewed.

paras: Devices commonly combine a lamp with a clock. Many ramp up light along a programmed curve, some include a dusk mode that dims at bedtime, and many include sound alarms or radio [1]. Wikipedia describes two types used clinically: a naturalistic dawn imitating a spring sunrise but used in mid-winter, and a sigmoid-shaped dawn lasting 30 minutes to 2 hours [1]. A 2011 biomedical-engineering report described a sunrise alarm for hearing-impaired users that manipulates a bedside lamp's output and adds vibration and sound alarms [2].

Wikipedia says the concept was first patented in 1890 as a mechanical sunrise, with modern electronic units patented in 1973, and that David Avery of Columbia University ran clinical trials in the 1980s following laboratory work showing that animal circadian rhythms respond to the dim, gradually rising dawn signal [1]. A commercial dawn simulator was patented by Outside In (Cambridge, now Lumie) in 2005 [1].

The theory is that early-morning light is especially effective at advancing the body clock, and that rising light before waking lowers sleep depth and prompts the physiological arousal, including a cortisol rise, that precedes natural waking, so that sleepers wake by themselves at full brightness [1]. Dawn simulation generally uses 100 to 300 lux, far less than a 10,000-lux light box, and because the treatment completes before waking it may be a more convenient alternative to post-waking light therapy; Wikipedia notes that about 19 percent of patients stop post-awakening bright light therapy because of inconvenience [1].

Winter depression: a 1993 randomized crossover study in 16 people with recurrent autumn-winter symptoms but without major depression compared 4 days of a slow 45-minute dawn peaking at 100 lux with a rapid 4-second rise; the slow dawn improved subjective measures including energy, mood, social interest and productivity more than baseline or the rapid dawn [3]. A 1992 randomized crossover study of 7 winter-depression patients compared a week of bright (1700 lux) dawn simulation with a week of standard bright morning light; Hamilton scores fell from 18.9 to 6.6 with standard light but not significantly with bright dawn (18.0 to 11.3), and early-morning awakening was a frequent side effect of the bright dawn [4]. Other randomized trials compared dawn simulation with light boxes or bright light in seasonal affective disorder and paediatric seasonal depression [5][6][7][8]. Wikipedia summarises the comparison with bright light as mixed: some studies favour dawn simulation, others find no difference, and others favour bright light [1].

Reviews: a 2020 American Family Physician review lists commercial devices for light therapy or dawn simulation among options for seasonal affective disorder, noting that 2,500 to 10,000 lux for 30 to 60 minutes at the same time daily is typically effective for light therapy [9]. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of light interventions for sleep in circadian rhythm disorders and neuropsychiatric illness found improved sleep continuity (effect size -0.23), reduced self-reported sleep disturbance (-0.32) and advanced delayed sleep timing (-0.34); it covered light therapies in general, not wake-up lights specifically [10]. A review of sleep strategies in elite soccer players suggested dawn-simulation therapy before waking as a possibly beneficial sleep-hygiene measure [11].

Healthy and other groups: a 2013 study examined artificial dawn and morning blue light for effects on daytime cognitive performance, well-being, cortisol and melatonin [12]. A feasibility study in medical students evaluated a sunrise alarm clock intervention for perceived stress, burnout and sleep quality [13].

Dawn simulators are generally regarded as low risk. In the bright-dawn trial above, early-morning awakening was a frequent side effect [4]. Light before waking can shorten late sleep for some people, and a regular wake time is itself a component of any benefit. People with bipolar disorder or eye disease are generally advised to seek clinical advice before using light-based therapies for treatment.

The devices are discussed as one tool for a consistent wake time, in a bundle with blackout curtains, sleep masks and white noise. Claims about facial or skin benefits rest on the indirect link between regular sleep and appearance; the sources reviewed do not test sunrise alarms against appearance outcomes.

Features that vary include ramp length, maximum brightness, colour of the light, dusk mode, backup sound alarm and whether the clock is intended for clinical light therapy. Prices usually range from about $30 to $120.
